s: God, through Ezra, reproaches Israel for its ingratitude after all he did for them, and says he will turn to other nations who will believe.
God promises the kingdom to a new people. Ezra sees on Mount Zion a great crowd crowned and given palms by a young man taller than all: the Son of God.
The first vision. Thirty years after the city's fall, Ezra asks God why Israel suffers while Babylon, no better, prospers.
The angel Uriel answers that Ezra cannot understand even earthly things, much less God's ways, but says the age is hurrying to its end.
Signs of the end are foretold. Ezra fasts again and asks why God has handed over his one chosen people to the many nations.
God made the world and will bring it to its end himself. Ezra is told more signs and the coming of a new age.
Ezra asks why so few are saved. He is told of the Messiah's reign of 400 years, the resurrection and the judgment, and that the way to life is narrow.
God says that the world was made for the many but the age to come for the few. Ezra prays for mercy on sinners and is told to think of his own reward.
More signs of the end. Ezra sees a woman mourning her only son, who died on his wedding day.
As Ezra comforts her, the woman is changed into a shining city: she was Zion, and the vision shows its future glory.
In a dream Ezra sees an eagle rising from the sea, with twelve wings and three heads, ruling the whole earth.
A lion rebukes the eagle and it is burned up. The eagle is the fourth kingdom of Daniel's vision and the lion is the Messiah.
Ezra sees a man rise from the sea and fly with the clouds. He destroys the hostile nations with fire from his mouth and gathers a peaceful multitude: the Messiah and the ten lost tribes.
God speaks to Ezra from a bush and tells him to prepare. Ezra drinks a fiery cup and dictates for forty days, restoring the holy books that were burned, and many more.
A Christian addition. God foretells war and disaster on the nations that persecute his people, especially Egypt, Babylon and Asia.
Woes on Babylon, Asia, Egypt and Syria. God's people are told to endure persecution, to live as strangers in the world, and to trust in his deliverance.
i: 4 Esdras (called 2 Esdras in Protestant Bibles, and Ezra Sutuel in the Ethiopian Bible, where it is Scripture) is an apocalypse: a book of visions. Its core, chapters 3 to 14, was written by a Jewish author around AD 100, soon after the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. Christians later added chapters 1 and 2 and 15 and 16 at the beginning and end.

In it Ezra, grieving over the ruined city, asks the angel Uriel the hardest questions of faith: why does God let his people suffer, why are so few saved, what becomes of the dead? Seven visions follow: a mourning woman who becomes a shining city, an eagle with many wings rebuked by a lion, a man rising from the sea. In the last chapter Ezra rewrites the lost holy books from memory.

The Church does not read it as Scripture, yet its words have entered her prayer: the Introit of the Requiem Mass, “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them”, echoes 4 Esdras 2:34-35. It is printed here because the 1609 Douay kept it in an appendix.
